lead: At the centre of today’s readings stands one question: can God be trusted? Abram, still childless, is taken outside to look at the stars, and he believes. In John, the crowds argue about where Jesus comes from, and he tells them that he comes from the one who sent him. Beside these, the Gibeonites deceive Joshua in the second reading because the leaders “did not ask direction from the Lord”, and Paul ends his long reflection on Israel with praise, for “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable”. It is also a First Friday, when many families turn to the Heart of Jesus, in whom God’s faithfulness has a human face.

set: Years have passed since the first promise, and Abram has no child. By the custom of the time, a childless man’s heir might be a servant of his household, and Abram names Eliezer of Damascus (15:2). This is the first time in the story that Abram answers God, and his first words are a complaint. Many scholars think that the chapter joins two scenes: the promise of an heir (vv. 1–6) and the promise of the land (vv. 7–21).

The reading ends at v. 15, just before the climax, when a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch pass between the divided animals (15:17). Jeremiah 34:18 shows the meaning of such a rite: those who pass between the pieces accept the fate of the animals if they break their word.
str: v. 1: the vision: “Do not be afraid”.
vv. 7–11: the land, and the animals prepared.
vv. 12–15: a deep sleep, and a word about slavery and return.
kw: From the same root as “amen”. It means to lean on, to hold firm. Abram rests his whole weight on God’s word.
To count, to credit as to an account. God treats this trust as the right relationship with him.
In the Old Testament this is faithfulness to a relationship. The POC has nīthīkaraṇam, “justification”, which already points to St Paul’s use of the verse.
vv: Do not be afraid, Abram, I am your shield;
The chapter opens with the words God so often speaks to those he calls. Abram has just come back from a war, and God himself will be his shield.
Look toward heaven and count the stars, if you are able to count them.
God brings an old man out of his tent and gives him the night sky. Nothing has changed in Abram’s house, and nothing will for many years. The promise is all he has.
And he believed the Lord; and the Lord reckoned it to him as righteousness.

One of the great verses of the Bible. St Paul builds on it in Romans 4:3 and Galatians 3:6. St James quotes it too, and adds that Abraham’s “faith was active along with his works” (James 2:22–23). Abraham’s faith is God’s gift, and by grace it bears fruit in obedience.
ch: The Catechism says that Abraham thus fulfils the definition of faith in Hebrews 11:1 (CCC 146), and calls him the father of all who believe. Justification comes from God’s grace, and it is given to those who believe, and calls us to cooperate by faith and works of charity (CCC 1987–2005). Nostra Aetate 4 and CCC 839 remember that Israel is still loved by God for the sake of the patriarchs, as today’s epistle says.

set: Jesus has gone up in the middle of the festival and is teaching openly in the Temple (7:14). People from the city are surprised that the authorities do nothing. Their question shows a real belief of some Jews of the time, found in writings outside the Bible: that the Messiah would stay hidden until the moment of his appearing. Others held a different view, as later in the chapter some say that he must come from Bethlehem (7:42; Micah 5:2).
str: vv. 25–27: the people of Jerusalem wonder, and raise an objection.
vv. 28–29: Jesus cries out: “I have not come on my own”.
v. 30: an attempted arrest fails: his hour has not yet come.
kw: A loud, public cry, used also in 7:37 and 12:44. In John it marks a solemn word from Jesus.
In John this is the hour of the Cross and glory (see 12:23; 13:1; 17:1). Until it comes, no one can touch him.
John’s word for the miracles, which point beyond themselves to who Jesus is.
vv: Yet we know where this man is from; but when the Messiah comes, no one will know where he is from.
John loves this kind of irony. They know Nazareth, and they think that settles the matter. They do not know where he is really from. The reader, who has read John 1:1–18, does know.
I have not come on my own. But the one who sent me is true, and you do not know him.
This is what the discussion has been missing. The question is not his home town but the one who sent him.
but no one laid hands on him, because his hour had not yet come.
His life is not in the hands of his enemies. He will give it when the time comes (see John 10:18). Only God sets that hour.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Son came down from heaven to do the will of the Father who sent him (CCC 606), and that the hour of Jesus is the hour when he passes to the Father and gives the Spirit (CCC 729–730). The Creed answers the question of the crowd: he is “God from God, begotten, not made”, and also a man of Nazareth, of the Virgin Mary.

study: What promise of God have I waited for so long that I have nearly stopped believing it? What would it mean to look at the stars again?
Do I think I know Jesus so well that I have stopped asking who he is?
